title: Volume to draw up from an ampoule (mg in 1 mL, mg in 2 mL)
blurb: Read an ampoule label correctly and calculate the volume to draw up, whether the strength is per 1 mL, per 2 mL or in micrograms.
question: A person is prescribed 7.5 mg of a medicine by intramuscular injection. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up?

teach.h: The ampoule label is want ÷ have × volume
teach.body: Formal rule: volume to draw up = (dose prescribed ÷ amount in the ampoule) × volume of the ampoule. Plain English: the label tells you how many mg are in how many mL. Work out what fraction of the ampoule's drug you need, and draw up that fraction of its volume. Part A has three injection items, and "X mg in 1 mL" and "X mg in 2 mL" labels appear on every practice paper.
teach.cite: FACTS.md sections 1 and 4; Pearson VUE NMC practice papers

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Hughes on a surgical ward
teach.body: Owen Hughes, 58, is prescribed 7.5 mg of a medicine IM. The ampoule reads 10 mg in 2 mL. Volume = 7.5 ÷ 10 × 2 = 0.75 × 2 = 1.5 mL. Sense-check: 7.5 mg is three-quarters of the ampoule's 10 mg, so three-quarters of its 2 mL. Type 1.5 mL.

teach.h: Per 2 mL is not per 1 mL

teach.text: Treating "10 mg in 2 mL" as 10 mg in 1 mL: forgetting to multiply by the ampoule's 2 mL halves the volume and gives half the dose. Read the volume on the label every time.

items.label: recheck the sum and the route

teach.caption: Teaching guide only; maximum IM volumes vary by site and local policy.

children.label: 150 mg from 100 mg in 2 mL = 3 mL

teach.body: Injection volume items ask for the unit: type the number and mL, to the decimal places asked, with a leading zero below 1 (0.5 mL) and no trailing zero (1.5 mL, not 1.50 mL). Round only at the end.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice tests, answer-format guidance

items: "X mg in 2 mL" means multiply by 2; "in 1 mL" by 1.
Match micrograms and mg before dividing.
Classic error: reading a per-2 mL label as per 1 mL (half the dose).
Sense-check: most IM and SC volumes are 0.1 to 5 mL.

summary: You can now calculate the volume to draw up from any ampoule label, including per 2 mL strengths and microgram labels, and check the result is a plausible injection volume typed in Pearson's format.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the ampoule's 2 mL.
whyNot.3: Drew up the whole ampoule, which holds 10 mg.

A.q: A service user is prescribed lorazepam 2 mg by intramuscular injection. The ampoule label reads 4 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Multiplied by 2 as if the label were per 2 mL.
whyNot.2: Misread 4 mg as 0.4 mg, a tenfold error.

whyNot.3: Used 10 mg (the strength per mL) as if it were the amount in 2 mL.

C.q: A person is prescribed 250 micrograms of a medicine by subcutaneous injection. The ampoule label reads 1 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the ampoule's 2 mL.
whyNot.2: No conversion: micrograms treated as mg, giving 500 mL.

C.q: A person is prescribed 150 mg of a medicine by intravenous injection. The ampoules available each read 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: Volume = 150 ÷ 100 × 2 = 1.5 × 2 = 3 mL (two ampoules opened, 1 mL of the second discarded).

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the ampoule's 2 mL.
whyNot.3: Drew up one whole ampoule, which holds only 100 mg.

whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

reteach.title: Read the mL on the label
reteach.question: An ampoule reads 100 mg in 2 mL. How many mg are in 1 mL?

blocks.body: "100 mg in 2 mL" means the whole 2 mL ampoule holds 100 mg, so 1 mL holds 50 mg. Use the label as written: want ÷ 100 × 2. Or convert to 50 mg per mL: want ÷ 50. Both give the same volume.

blocks.text: 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8 is the fraction of the ampoule. The volume is 0.8 × 2 = 1.6 mL.

explain.body: When the label says "in 1 mL", the volume is simply want ÷ have.

whyNot.1: Multiplied by 2 as if the label were per 2 mL.
whyNot.2: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

test.q: A person is prescribed 0.5 mg of a medicine by subcutaneous injection. The ampoule label reads 250 micrograms in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: 0.5 mg was taken as 5000 micrograms, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: 0.5 mg was taken as 50 micrograms, a tenfold slip.

explain.body: If the dose is more than the ampoule holds, the volume is more than the ampoule's volume. 40 mg from 20 mg in 2 mL must be more than 2 mL.
